commentary.seminaVerbi:
Paul’s “more excellent way” reads like a psychological claim: the self can perform brilliance and sacrifice as a kind of armor, but only love dissolves the performer and makes the act real. That aligns with the Bhagavad Gita’s karma-yoga, where action without grasping at its fruit purifies the agent; with Mahayana Buddhism’s bodhicitta and the bodhisattva vow, where insight and powers are secondary to compassion; and with Sufism’s insistence that ecstatic gifts mean little without adab and the heart’s tenderness.

“Through a glass, darkly” has a close cousin in Plato’s cave and in the Upanishadic neti neti: cognition is partial, maturity is the slow surrender of childish certainty. Speculation: it also resembles Zen’s distrust of spiritual fireworks—kōan practice as a stripping of cleverness until direct seeing.

Luke’s children in the marketplace echoes the Tao Te Ching’s refusal to be managed by expectations: the sage won’t dance on command or mourn on cue. It also touches Stoic independence from the crowd’s verdict and the Zen image of “no rank,” where both ascetic severity and convivial ease get misread by the same hungry cynicism.

“Wisdom is justified by her children” parallels the pragmatic test in Confucianism—virtue known by its fruits in conduct and harmony—and, speculatively, William James’s measure of truth by lived consequences rather than by applause.
commentary.excursus:
Paul’s “more excellent way” reads like an intervention for addicts of greatness. Tongues, prophecy, knowledge, even martyrdom: the whole spiritual achievement economy. He doesn’t deny the rush; he calls it noise. Without charity the self stays intact, and that intact self is the real idol—burning, giving, speaking, dazzling, all to keep the interior throne occupied.

Charity here is not sweetness; it is ego-death stretched over time. Patient, kind, not ambitious: a portrait of someone refusing the narcotic of being right, admired, or indispensable. “Beareth all things” sounds holy until you hear the dread in it: love as the capacity to remain present when your story of yourself is collapsing.

Luke’s scene is the same sickness in public. The generation wants religion as a performance keyed to their mood: play the flute, stage the funeral, give us the correct affect. John’s refusal of pleasure is demonized; Jesus’ embrace of pleasure is demonized. The complaint is identical because the desire is identical: control. They don’t want wisdom; they want a god who dances on command.

So “wisdom is justified by all her children” lands like a cold verdict. Wisdom doesn’t win arguments; it produces lives. Charity is the only “gift” that can’t be used to posture, because the moment you use it that way it turns back into brass and cymbal. The text isn’t consoling; it’s stripping you of every impressive refuge until only the terrifying simplicity remains: love, or nothing.
commentary.synthesis: Charity is the eschatological measure that renders every gift, feat, and posture accountable. Christ exposes a generation that judges by mood, while God judges by the fruit of wisdom.

gospel.text: Jesus frames the generation as a problem of judgment, not information: they refuse any form that would indict them, and the only vindication offered is the long audit of wisdom’s outcomes.

reading.text: Paul relocates authority from present competencies to eschatological completion: partial knowledge cannot found ultimacy, so the community’s hierarchy of “better gifts” is relativized by the coming of the perfect.
The child/man contrast is not sentiment but epistemic discipline: maturity is measured by what one discards, and the triad that remains is ordered toward a single summit.

marginalia.text: Gifts are bait; the “way” is the trapdoor under them.
Angelic speech without love: liturgy reduced to percussion.
Mountain-moving faith can still be a zero.
Almsgiving and martyrdom can be self-investment with no return.
Love is described by negations: it is known by what it refuses.
Charity outlives the spectacular; the permanent judges the temporary.
“Known” precedes knowing; the subject is already read.
They demand a controllable Messiah: dance on cue, weep on cue.
Asceticism is pathologized: holiness rebranded as possession.
Feasting is criminalized: mercy rebranded as vice.
Wisdom’s defense is not argument but offspring—results.

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: O God, who set over your people, as selfless shepherds and fearless martyrs, Saints Cyprian and Cornelius, grant us, through their intercession, strength of spirit and of faith to work zealously for the unity of your Church. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God for ever and ever.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Matins

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: O God, who set over your people, as selfless shepherds and fearless martyrs, Saints Cyprian and Cornelius, grant us, through their intercession, strength of spirit and of faith to work with zeal for the unity of your Church. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Lauds

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: Lord, holy Father, faithful God, who sent the promised Holy Spirit to gather together the people whom sin had scattered, help us to be, in the midst of the world, a leaven of unity and peace. Through Jesus Christ our Lord.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Terce

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: Almighty and loving God, who at the midpoint of our day grant rest from our weariness, look with favor upon the work we have begun today, remedy our shortcomings, and make our deeds pleasing to you. Through Jesus Christ our Lord.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Sext

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, who for the salvation of mankind stretched out your arms upon the cross, grant that all our actions may be pleasing to you and serve to make your redemption known to the world. You who live and reign for ever and ever.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Nones

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: O God, who set Saints Cyprian and Cornelius over your people as selfless shepherds and fearless martyrs, grant us, through their intercession, strength of spirit and faith to work zealously for the unity of your Church. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Vespers

hoursOfPrayer.prayer:
Let us pray:
Lord Jesus Christ, you are meek and humble of heart and you offer those who come to you a yoke that is easy and a burden that is light; deign, then, to accept the desires and the deeds of the day we have ended. Grant that we may rest during the night, so that, with body and spirit renewed, we may persevere steadfastly in your service. You who live and reign for ever and ever.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Compline

lines: But be zealous for the better gifts. And I shew unto you yet a more excellent way.
If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.
And if I should have prophecy and should know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I should have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.
And if I should distribute all my goods to feed the poor, and if I should deliver my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.
Charity is patient, is kind: charity envieth not, dealeth not perversely, is not puffed up,
Is not ambitious, seeketh not her own, is not provoked to anger, thinketh no evil:
Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth with the truth:
Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.
Charity never falleth away: whether prophecies shall be made void or tongues shall cease or knowledge shall be destroyed.
For we know in part: and we prophesy in part.
But when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away.
When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child. But, when I became a man, I put away the things of a child.
We see now through a glass in a dark manner: but then face to face. Now I know in part: but then I shall know even as I am known.
And now there remain faith, hope, and charity, these three: but the greatest of these is charity.
readings.heading: A reading from the First Letter of St. Paul to Corinthians

lines: And the Lord said: Whereunto then shall I liken the men of this generation? And to what are they like?
They are like to children sitting in the marketplace and speaking one to another and saying: We have piped to you, and you have not danced: we have mourned, and you have not wept.
For John the Baptist came neither eating bread nor drinking wine. And you say: He hath a devil.
The Son of man is come eating and drinking. And you say: Behold a man that is a glutton and a drinker of wine, a friend of publicans and sinners.
And wisdom is justified by all her children.
readings.heading: From the Gospel according to Luke
